messages.subject: Information heterogeneity across hierarchies
parts:
Hi,

I have a hierarchical model where there are individuals at the bottom, organised into species at the mid-level, then into genera at the top. For some species I have considerably more data sets than I do for others. This means that some of the mid-level parameters are poorly/non-identified. For others, the data is sufficient to identify these parameters. 

I really like using a hierarchical model for this particular application, due to the natural ordering, however I am running up against the difficulty that the overall samplers fail to converge due to the heterogeneity in information across species.

Does anyone have any suggestions on what to do here? I ideally don't want to jettison those species for which I have low amounts of data, (since this information could be shared across genera), but also don't want to end up with rubbish because the MCMC doesn't converge.

Best,

Ben

messages.subject: Information heterogeneity across hierarchies
parts: With multi level hierarchies you really need priors with sensible implications at all levels, as well as tricks like centered parameterizations... So I'm afraid the solution is model specific. Krzysztof

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Information heterogeneity across hierarchies
parts:
Yes, one of the awkward features of deep hierarchical models (with many layers,
we usually reserve levels to speak about different effects on the same layer)
is that variance grows exponentially fast so you have to have tighter priors than
you might initially consider. For example, try sampling from the hierarchical prior
and see how much variance you get. This is also a nice way to tune the priors
to ensure reasonable variance of the top-level parameters.

As Krzysztof notes you’ll also want to be careful about the implementation.
There are 2^{nodes} possible parameterizations but a fully non-centered
one will probably be a good starting point. You’ll ultimately get something
that looks like

top_level_effect = mean_effect + \prod_{n = 1}^{N_layers} standard_deviation_{n}
